div.font: Appendix D (3/5)
Purpose, Explanation, and Arbitrariness

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe flex-start; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 796px; height: 1px; padding-top: 98px; margin-left: 28px;

div.font: - "Purpose only exists in the mind/imagination."
- "Meaning is imagined, not real."
- The idea of reality having a "meaning" is only us falsely projecting "purpose" onto reality, and it doesn't really exist [ontologically].
- Applying what is in the imagination to reality is a category error, for imagination does not necessarily describe reality.

- Either:
- The validity of the "if I can't [phenomenologicall]y feel/know/observe X, then it doesn't (or can't) exist" argument.
- The argument that "purpose exists only in the imagination, and so external/ontological purpose does not exist."
- Based on the "universe is arbitrary" claim, this also claims that there's no external will (in which, further commitments are addressed in that section).
- Imagination encompasses both what exists in reality and what does not, so the argument for this claim needs to align with their distinction.

font.b: How the Project Addresses These Commitments

div.font: - "If I can't

span.style: font-size: 11px; background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.span: phenomenologically feel/know/observe an external will (like I can with my own), then it doesn't (or can't) exist."

span.style: font-size: 11px; background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.span: - This line of reasoning equates perception with reality, which redefines "truth" to be relative to your perception (rather than an independent reality).

span.style: font-size: 11px; background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.span: - As such, this doesn't distinguish between truth and falsehood, for false perception exists - allowing falsehoods to be justified using the same argument.

span.style: font-size: 11px; background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.span: - If you reject defining truth by reality (ie. claiming that false perception does not exist), then you either reject our capacity for knowing any truth, or you accept that truth is entirely subjective -

span.style: background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255)); font-size: 11px;
background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255)); font-size: 11px;

div.span: Cost of Disagreement section in the project's conclusion for further commitments.

span.style: background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.font: - The argument for "purpose only exists in the imagination

span.style: font-size: 11px; background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.span: " needs to align with "false imaginations" rather than "true imaginations".

div.font: - The distinction between true and false imaginations is whether or not they are observed in reality. Moreover, the distinction between true and false imaginations that cannot be seen or comprehended (as with metaphysical concepts) is whether or not there exists a rationally grounded definition.

- The definition of an "external will" is derived from applying pattern recognition between the ordered, external effects in reality (from the precedent of our own internal wills) and the external order of reality (which - from the only example we have with our own wills - can only be explained by coming from another will).
- Moreover, the only meaningful [phenomenological] definition for "reality" is anything that resists our will - which coherently explains this definition.

span.style: background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255)); font-size: 11px;

div.span: So, for this claim to be a better fit than the results of this project,

b.style: background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255)); font-size: 11px;

div.b: it will need to provide a rival definition for "reality" - one that still distinguishes between reality and perception

span.style: background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255)); font-size: 11px;

div.span: - while also showing that the link between our phenomenal wills and reality can't be used to explain the reality that we don't will.

div.font: - If you reject the distinction between reality and perception, then

span.style: font-size: 11px; background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.span: it's the "if I don't feel X, it doesn't exist" argument - see above.

span.b: 4. "Reality doesn't need purpose/will to explain its behavior."

b.style: background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255)); text-align: left;
background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255)); font-size: 12px;

div.font: - "The laws of physics just are."
- "The universe just is - no deeper explanation is required."
- Either:
- "Reality" can be rationally and completely understood without appealing to God (ie. some transcendent, conscious creator) for the answer.
- "What do we observe in reality?" is a more meaningful question than "why does reality exist?" or "what is reality's source?".

- Either:
- The validity of the "it just is" argument (ie. no further explanation is needed to answer the question).

- If you allow "it just is" to also answer any question (like "why do apples fall?" or "why do I feel pain?"), then this claim rejects the concept of external purpose/causation for all things - for there is no cause or explanation that is behind anything we phenomenally experience.

- Otherwise (if you can ask "why" for simpler questions, but not for reality itself), then the requirements for asking "why" to any question needs to be established first, before addressing this claim.
- Given that "purpose" comes from "will", then the only limit to asking "why" is to "will" itself (ie. it is a category error to ask, "why did the will do that?")

span.style: font-size: 11px; background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.span: The question being addressed is, "what is the ultimate source of reality?" - and as such, responding to this with, "no answer is needed" is really saying, "the question is formulated wrong: it is a category error to associate 'source' with 'reality'."

font.b: How the Project Addresses These Commitments

div.font: - "There is no external purpose/causation

span.style: font-size: 11px; background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));
font-size: 11px; background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.span: - The only phenomenological observation we have of "causation" is our own wills affecting the reality we observe. As a result, it is the only rational precedent/ possibility for how reality exists is (ie. by some external purpose/causation) - meaning that a rational answer to the question of "reality's source" does exist.

span.style: font-size: 11px; background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.span: - As a result (given the existence of a rational answer for this question), this claim's line of reasoning

b.style: background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255)); font-size: 11px;

div.b: does not distinguish between truth and falsehood

span.style: background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255)); font-size: 11px;

div.span: , for falsehood can be justified in the exact same way (by countering a rational explanation with the rejection of the need for an answer).

span.style: background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255)); font-size: 11px;

div.span: - If you reject the concept of "reality's source" when a rational explanation exists, then arguing that reality "just is" is simply a preference to not answer the question - not a rational claim to be addressed.

span.style: background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.font: - "It is a category error to associate 'source' with 'reality' (ie. 'reality' is not a thing that can rationally have a 'source')

span.style: font-size: 11px; background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.font: - We derived the concept of "reality's source" from inferring "everything that begins comes from a source" (the ontological form of "all information comes from a source") and applying that principle to reality, as we also deduce that the universe had a beginning.
- Moreover, if "ontological nothing" exists, then it is irrational to claim that "the universe came from nothing", for the universe literally wouldn't have come from anything to begin with.

- So, if we can't apply the "every inference has a limit" inference to reality with the "the universe came from nothing" claim, then it must have come a "something" that is fundamentally a non-universe - ie. neither space nor time.
- As a result, the claim of "reality has no concept of a source" is not the best-fit explanation, as the "reality does have a source" claim is rationally grounded.

- If you reject the concept of "reality's source" when a rational definition exists, then arguing that reality "just is" validates a form of reasoning that does not distinguish between truth and falsehood (for all falsehoods lack rationally grounded definitions).
